quote: not the other kind
why: the sentence commits to "true answer" and then spends extra force denying a reading (a lie) nobody in the scene raised
suggestion: cut the denial and stop at the positive claim: "so Chloe decides it's a true answer."

quote: "I don't know, honey." Her mom doesn't look up when she says it
why: the not-looking-up is simultaneous with the speaking, so splitting them with a period reads as two events instead of one continuous beat
suggestion: "I don't know, honey," her mom says, not looking up.

quote: said sorry about four times standing in the kitchen with his keys already in his hand
why: loads a reported speech-act with a prepositional scene-setting explanation instead of splitting the physical detail into its own sentence
suggestion: He stood in the kitchen with his keys already in his hand and said sorry about four times.

rule_name: Use Past Perfect for Action Before the Narrative Present
quote: He tried to move two things this morning, couldn't move either one of them, then said sorry about four times
why: the narrative is present tense, so this account of an earlier-that-day event needs past perfect to mark it as antecedent instead of an unsignalled slide into simple past
suggestion: He had tried to move two things that morning, hadn't been able to move either one, then had said sorry about four times.

quote: She doesn't say that part out loud.
why: the previous sentence already marks the riff as thought ("which she thinks is funny"), so this restates what was already established as unspoken
suggestion: cut the sentence; the "she thinks" framing already did the job.

quote: Chloe notices the chair
why: routes an already-rendered detail (the chair the same size as hers) back through a perception verb instead of trusting the image
suggestion: cut the filter clause; the prior sentence already put the small chair on the page.

quote: because adults don't usually do that
why: a trailing "because" clause tacked on to explain the significance of the fact just stated, rather than letting the detail stand
suggestion: cut the clause and let the small chair speak for itself.

quote: "No." He says it straight away
why: the manner of delivery (straight away, without thinking) is simultaneous with the word, so the period splits one beat into two
suggestion: "No," he says straight away, without needing to think about it first.

rule_name: STYLE_RULES §8 Automatic-fail narrator constructions (trailing explanatory clause)
quote: which is not how her mom answers questions
why: a comparative verdict tacked on after the comma, telling the reader how to weigh the fact instead of stopping at the fact
suggestion: cut the clause; let "He says it straight away, without needing to think about it first" stand on its own.

quote: and she gets it fast, and her face goes hot in the good way, so she has to hold still until it stops
why: three clauses of unequal weight (getting it, getting it fast, the reaction) are strung together with coordinating "and" instead of subordination
suggestion: She gets the next one fast, and her face goes hot in the good way until she has to hold still to stop it.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: that one takes her a second
why: part of a chapter-wide pattern of "a second"/"a while" used as a generic duration marker regardless of what's being timed
suggestion: that one snags her

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: Ben stops writing for a second
why: another instance of the reflexive "for a second" duration filler reused for an unrelated moment
suggestion: Ben stops writing

quote: It is the easiest thing she has done all morning
why: weak "it is" opener that tells the reader a verdict instead of letting the description carry it
suggestion: The easiest thing she has done all morning, and she is bad at it.

rule_name: STYLE_RULES §8 Automatic-fail narrator constructions ("which is" evaluation)
quote: which is worse than finding out afterward
why: a "which is" clause that ranks/evaluates the preceding fact instead of stating it and stopping
suggestion: cut the clause; "She can tell she's bad at it while it is happening" already carries the weight.

quote: He doesn't write anything down. He doesn't ask a different question, and he doesn't do
why: three consecutive "he doesn't" openings stack negatives instead of restating the fact as one positive/negative statement
suggestion: He writes nothing down, asks nothing different, and lets the room go quiet instead of moving on to something easier.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: the thing where a grown-up says okay and moves on to something easier
why: "the thing where" is a named placeholder crutch standing in for behavior that should be shown directly
suggestion: he doesn't say okay and move on to something easier

rule_name: STYLE_RULES §2/§4 Register: figurative language belongs in mouths
quote: the quiet turns into the question instead
why: an invented, writerly personification of silence built by the narrator, not spoken or thought by a character
suggestion: and the room stays quiet long enough that the silence starts to feel like the question itself

quote: and this time she watches him do it, and it takes him longer than the other ones
why: two unequal clauses (watching, and the duration observation) chained with "and" rather than subordinated
suggestion: Ben writes that down; this time she watches him do it, and it takes longer than the other ones.

rule_name: STYLE_RULES §8 Automatic-fail narrator constructions (repeated frame verb/anaphora)
quote: There is a set of questions about what you would do if you found somebody's wallet
why: "There is/are" opens four sentences in this one paragraph (pictures, questions, timed sheet, maze), a repeated frame the reader starts to hear as a tic
suggestion: vary the openers: "A set of questions asks what you'd do if you found somebody's wallet...", "Another timed sheet has rows of shapes...", "One has a maze on it."

quote: which turns out not to have been necessary
why: a trailing "which" clause that evaluates the preceding detail's importance instead of stopping at the fact
suggestion: cut the clause: "including the part about the neighbor."

quote: for a second longer than he has looked at her all morning
why: mirrors the guide's own cut example ("for a second longer than the question needed") almost verbatim, a tail that tells the reader how to read the look instead of stating it
suggestion: Ben looks at her, longer than usual.

quote: She hears her mom say the teacher says.
why: routes the overheard fragment through the banned filter verb "hears" instead of rendering the sound directly
suggestion: Her mom's voice: the teacher says.

quote: She hears Ben say a lot of words she doesn't have.
why: a second consecutive "hears" filter in the same passage, the exact construction the rule names and bans
suggestion: Ben's voice runs on, full of words she doesn't have.

quote: There's nothing wrong with her.
why: Ben repeats the mother's question back almost verbatim as his answer, adding no new information
suggestion: Nothing's wrong.

quote: Nobody's calling you about handwriting.
why: restates, verbatim in substance, the point just made in the same speech ("not what anybody in that building is calling you about") with no new information
suggestion: cut the second sentence and let the first stand.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: Nobody says anything for a while.
why: "for a while" used again as a generic universal duration marker, part of the chapter-wide pattern
suggestion: Nobody says anything.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: doesn't start it for a second
why: third reflexive use of "for a second" as a generic duration filler across the chapter, for yet another unrelated moment
suggestion: doesn't start it right away

rule_name: STYLE_RULES §5/§8 The trailing clause / pointing at the scene
quote: the way she does
why: a trailing tail asserting habitualness without evidence, signalling "this is a pattern, notice it" rather than stating the fact and stopping, echoing the guide's own cut example "which nobody at that school does"
suggestion: cut the tail: "Chloe has her seatbelt across her with both hands holding it away from her neck."

quote: "He didn't give me a number." Her mom says it to the windshield.
why: the manner of delivery (to the windshield, not to Chloe) is simultaneous with the line, so the period splits one continuous evasive beat into two
suggestion: "He didn't give me a number," her mom says to the windshield.

quote: Chloe knows that isn't true
why: opens with the banned filter verb "knows" to state a bare conclusion before the reasoning that follows
suggestion: That isn't true, not with a word like that; nobody hands one over without a number stuck to it.

quote: Nobody at the school says anything to her about the Wednesday, so as far as she can tell nobody in the building knows it happened
why: reports a universal absence of reaction/knowledge as evidence the event went unnoticed, rather than showing one specific detail of the building's inattention
suggestion: Mrs. Aldana doesn't mention it. Nobody at her table mentions it. As far as Chloe can tell, that's the whole building.

rule_name: STYLE_RULES §13 Guide 2 checklist #11 (Chloe explains her own behavior to the reader)
quote: which is that if you finish first, then sit still, then don't say anything to anybody, nobody talks to you at all
why: the narration has Chloe spell out the mechanism of her own coping strategy directly to the reader as a stated rule, rather than letting the reader infer it from behavior
suggestion: let the behavior carry it: cut the explanatory "which is that..." clause and show the strategy through a specific instance instead of a formula.

quote: Not the teacher, not the kids at your table, nobody.
why: three stacked negatives in a row, closely mirroring the guide's own cut example ("Nobody makes an announcement, nobody says anything at breakfast")
suggestion: restate as one positive statement: "Nobody talks to her, not the teacher, not the kids at her table."

rule_name: STYLE_RULES §8 Automatic-fail narrator constructions (repeated frame verb/anaphora)
quote: It works on a Monday, it works on a Thursday, it works in reading, it works in math
why: the frame "it works" repeats four times in one sentence, the anaphora fail the automatic-fail table names directly
suggestion: It works on a Monday and a Thursday, in reading and in math, every day until the end of the year.

quote: it's the whole thing
why: "the whole thing" is named directly in the rule's title as a vague abstraction standing in for a specific, nameable understanding
suggestion: she only knows that being quiet is what makes her disappear
